His saying, exalted is He: ﴿from a despised fluid﴾, that is, weak; ﴿then We placed it in a secure place﴾, meaning the womb; ﴿for a known period﴾, which is the duration of pregnancy; ﴿and We determined [it]﴾. The people of Medina and al-Kisa'i recited "faqaddarna" with a shadda. The rest recited it with a light pronunciation. Is there a difference between them?

Regarding this there are two opinions.
One: they are two dialects with one meaning. al-Farra' said: the Arabs say: "qadara 'alayhi" and "qaddara 'alayhi." Those who recited with the light pronunciation argued: if it were with a shadda, He would have said: "fa-ni'ma al-muqaddirun." al-Farra' answered: the Arabs may combine the two dialects, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So give respite to the disbelievers; give them a little respite﴾ [al-Tariq: 17]. The poet said:

"She denied me, and what she denied was only the graying hair and the baldness."

He says: she denied nothing except what happens among people.

The second: the light form is from "power" (qudrah) and "possession" (milk), and the heavy form is from "measuring" (taqdir) and "decree" (qada'). Then He made clear to them His workmanship so that they might take warning and affirm His oneness. So He said, exalted is He: ﴿Have We not made the earth a gatherer﴾ (kifatan). The linguists said: kaft in the language means gathering together. The meaning is that it gathers its inhabitants, living upon its back and dead in its belly. Ibn Qutaybah said: it is said: "iktif hadha ilayka," that is, gather it to you. They used to call the cemetery of al-Baqi' al-Gharqad "kiftah," because it is a graveyard that gathers the dead.

Regarding His saying, exalted is He: ﴿the living and the dead﴾, there are two opinions.
One: the meaning is: it gathers them, living and dead. This was said by the majority. al-Farra' said: "the living and the dead" are accusative by the falling of the gathering upon them, as if you said: "Have We not made the earth a gathering place of living and dead?" When you put tanwin, you put them in the accusative, as is recited: ﴿or feeding on a day of hunger﴾ ﴿an orphan﴾ [al-Balad: 14]. al-Akhfash said: it is in the accusative as a state (hal).
The second opinion: the meaning is: Have We not made the earth living through vegetation and cultivation, and dead through ruin and dryness? This is the view of Mujahid and Abu 'Ubaydah.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We placed in it firm mountains﴾ (rawasi). The explanation of ﴿towering﴾ (shamikhat), that is, lofty, has already been given. ﴿And We gave you to drink﴾ (asqaynakum): the meaning of "asqayna" has already been given [al-Hijr: 22; al-Jinn: 16], and the meaning of "al-furat" [al-Furqan: 53; Fatir: 12]. The meaning is: these things are more wondrous than resurrection. Then He mentioned what will be said to them in the Hereafter: ﴿Depart to that which you used to deny﴾ in the world, which is the Fire. ﴿Depart to a shade﴾. The majority recited this second word with a kasra on the lam as an imperative. Ubayy ibn Ka'b, (p-450) Abu 'Imran, and Ruways on the authority of Ya'qub recited it with a fatha on the lam as a report in the past tense. Ibn Qutaybah said: "al-zill" here is a shade of the smoke of the Fire of Hell, which rose and then split into three parts; likewise, the nature of great smoke when it rises is that it branches out. It will be said to them: "Remain in it until the reckoning is finished," just as the friends of God are in the shade of His Throne, or wherever He wills of the shade. Then each group is ordered to its place of abode, Paradise or Hell. ﴿Neither shady﴾, that is, it does not shade you from the heat of this Day, but rather brings you near the blaze of the Fire, to what is more severe for you than the heat of the sun. Mujahid said: it will be a branch above the person, a branch on his right, and a branch on his left, encompassing him. al-Dahhak said: the three branches are al-Dari', al-Zaqqum, and al-Ghislin. According to this view, this will be after entering the Fire.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and it will not avail against the flame﴾, that is, it will not ward off from you the blaze of Hell. Then He described the Fire, saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, it throws up sparks﴾, which is the plural of sharrah, that which flies off from the fire, scattered; ﴿like a castle﴾ (al-qasr). The majority recited with a sukun on the sad, as the singular of the palaces (qusur) that are built. This meaning is in the narration of Ibn Abi Talhah from Ibn 'Abbas, and it is the view of the majority. Ibn 'Abbas, Abu Razin, Mujahid, and Abu al-Jawza' recited "kal-qasar" with a fatha on the sad. In the singular reports of al-Bukhari from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas, he said: "We used to lift wood, a cask of three cubits or less, and lift it for winter, and we called it al-qasar." Ibn Qutaybah said: by the fatha on the sad he meant the roots of cut palm trees, uprooted. al-Zajjaj said: he meant the necks of camels. Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, 'A'ishah, 'Ikrimah, Abu Mijlaz, Abu al-Mutawakkil, and Ibn Ya'mar recited "kal-qasir" with a fatha on the qaf and a kasra on the sad. Ibn Mas'ud, Abu Hurayrah, and al-Nakha'i recited "kal-qusur" with a damma on both the qaf and the sad. Abu al-Darda', and Sa'id ibn (p-451) Jubayr recited "kal-qisar" with a kasra on the qaf and a fatha on the sad. Abu al-'Aliyah, Abu 'Imran, Abu Nuhayk, and Mu'adh al-Qari' recited "kal-qusr" with a damma on the qaf and a sukun on the sad.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿As if they were yellow camels﴾ (jimalatun). Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, and Abu Bakr on the authority of 'Asim recited "jimalatun" with an alif and a kasra on the jim. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Hafs on the authority of 'Asim recited "jimalatun" in the singular. Ruways on the authority of Ya'qub recited "jumalatun" with a damma on the jim. Abu Razin, Humayd, and Abu Haywah recited "jumalatun" with a damma on the jim in the singular. al-Zajjaj said: whoever recited "jimalatun" with a kasra is the plural of jimal, as you say: buyut and buyutat, and it is the plural of the plural, so the meaning is: as if the sparks were like the camels. Whoever recited "jumalatun" with a damma is the plural of "jumalah," and whoever recited "jumalatun" is the plural of jamal and jimalah, as it is said: hajar and hijarah, and dhakar and dhikarah. And "jumalatun" has been read, in the manner we explained, as "jumalatun" with a damma. And "al-sufr" here means the black ones. It is said of black camels that tend toward yellow: "ibil sufr." al-Farra' said: "al-sufr" are the black camels; a black camel is never seen except that it has a tinge of yellow, and so the Arabs called black camels "sufr," just as they called gazelles "adam" because of the darkness that overspreads their whiteness.

This is the Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 77, verses 1–50 (part 2 of 2):

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿This is a day when they will not speak﴾. The exegetes said: This is during some of the stations of the Resurrection. ʿIkrimah said: They spoke and disputed, then a seal was placed upon their mouths, and their hands and their feet spoke, and then they will not speak with any argument that benefits them. Abu Rajaʾ, al-Qasim ibn Muhammad, al-Aʿmash, and Ibn Abi ʿAblah read "This is a day when they will not speak" with a fatha on the mim (ALA: yawma, in the accusative).

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿This is the Day of Decision﴾, that is, between the people of Paradise and the people of Hellfire. ﴿We have gathered you﴾, meaning the deniers of this nation, ﴿and the former peoples﴾ of the deniers who denied their prophets. (p-452) ﴿So if you have a scheme, then scheme against Me﴾. Yaʿqub kept the yaʾ in both states (ALA: fakidūni). That is: if you are able to devise a plan, then devise one for yourselves.

Then He mentioned what belongs to the believers, saying: ﴿Indeed, the God-fearing will be in shades﴾, meaning the shade of trees and the shade of the shelters of palaces, ﴿and springs﴾ of water. This has already been explained, up to His saying: ﴿Eat﴾, that is, it will be said to them: Eat and drink with pleasure for what you used to do in the world by obeying Allah. Then He said to the disbelievers of Makkah: ﴿Eat and enjoy yourselves for a little while﴾ in this world until the end of your appointed terms, ﴿indeed you are criminals﴾, that is, polytheists against Allah.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And when it is said to them, "Bow down"﴾, concerning which there are two views.
The first: that it is when they are called to prostrate on the Day of Resurrection; this was related by al-ʿAwfi from Ibn ʿAbbas.
The second: that in this world, when it was said to them, "Bow down," that is, "Pray," ﴿they do not bow down﴾, that is, they do not pray. Mujahid and others held this view, and it is the most sound. It was also said: it was revealed concerning Thaqif, when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ commanded them to pray, and they said: "We will not bow, for it is a reproach upon us." He said: "There is no good in a religion that has no bowing in it."

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Then in what statement after this will they believe?﴾, that is: if they do not believe in this Qur'an, then in what Book after it will they believe? There is no Book after it.

Completed, by the help and success of Allah the Exalted, is the eighth part of the book "Zad al-Masir fi ʿIlm al-Tafsir" by the Imam Ibn al-Jawzi; and following it is the ninth part, whose beginning is the tafsir of the surah of

(p-443) Surah al-Mursalat (The Emissaries)

It is Meccan in its entirety according to the majority. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah, and Muqatil that it contains one Medinan verse, which is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when it is said to them, "Bow down," they do not bow down﴾ [al-Mursalat: 48].

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿By those sent forth successively﴾ [al-Mursalat: 1]. Regarding it there are four opinions.

The first: they are the winds, following one another. This was narrated by Abu al-'Ubaydayn from Ibn Mas'ud, and by al-'Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas. Mujahid and Qatadah also said this.

The second: they are the angels who are sent with what is good (al-ma'ruf) of God's command and prohibition. This was narrated by Masruq from Ibn Mas'ud. Abu Hurayrah and Muqatil also said this. al-Farra' said: they are the angels.

As for His saying, ﴿successively﴾ ('urfan), it is said: they are sent with what is good, and it is said: they follow one another like the mane (' urf) of a horse. The Arabs say: "The people ride to so-and-so 'urfan wahidan," when they set out towards him in great numbers. Ibn Qutaybah said: he means that the angels follow one another in what they are sent with. Its root is the mane of a horse, because it is a level line, one part following the next, so it was borrowed for a people who follow one another.

(p-445) The third: they are the messengers, by the signs (mu'jizat) by which they are recognized. This is the meaning of the saying of Abu Salih, mentioned by al-Zajjaj.

The fourth: the angels and the wind. This was said by Abu 'Ubaydah, who said: the meaning of "'urfan" is that they follow one another. It is said: "They came to me 'urfan." 

Regarding ﴿the stormy blasts﴾ (al-'asifat) there are two opinions.
One: they are the violently blowing winds. This is what the majority said.
The second: they are the angels. This was said by Muslim ibn Subayh. al-Zajjaj said: they seize (ta'sif) the soul of the disbeliever.

Regarding ﴿those that spread [clouds]﴾ (al-nashirat) there are five opinions.
One: they are the winds that spread the clouds. This was said by Ibn Mas'ud and the majority.
The second: they are the angels that spread the books. This was said by Abu Salih.
The third: the pages (suhuf) that are spread before God, exalted is He, with the deeds of the servants. This was said by al-Dahhak.
The fourth: the resurrection for the Judgment, in which the souls are spread out. This was said by al-Rabi'.
The fifth: the rain, which spreads the vegetation. This is reported by al-Mawardi.

(p-446) Regarding ﴿those that separate [truth from falsehood]﴾ (al-fariqat) there are four opinions.
One: the angels who bring what distinguishes between truth and falsehood. This was said by most of them.
The second: the verses of the Qur'an, which separated between the lawful and the unlawful. This was said by al-Hasan, Qatadah, and Ibn Kaysan.
The third: the wind, which separates the clouds and scatters them. This was said by Mujahid.
The fourth: the messengers. This was reported by al-Zajjaj.

Regarding ﴿those that deliver a reminder﴾ (fa'l-mulqiyat dhikra) there are two opinions.
One: the angels, who deliver to the prophets what they have borne of revelation. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah, and the majority.
The second: the messengers, who convey what was revealed to them to the nations. This was said by Qutrub.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿as an excuse or a warning﴾ ('udhran aw nudhran). Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, and Abu Bakr on the authority of 'Asim recited "'udhran" with a light pronunciation and "nudhran" with a heavy one. Abu 'Amr, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Hafs, and Khalaf recited both "'udhran" and "nudhran" with light pronunciation. al-Farra' said: it is a verbal noun (masdar), whether heavy or light. Its accusative is in the sense: they were sent with what they were sent with as an excuse from God and a warning. al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is: "those that deliver an excuse or a warning." It is also possible that the meaning is: "those that deliver a reminder, as an excuse and a warning." These mentioned things are in the genitive by the oath. The answer to the oath is ﴿What you are promised will surely occur﴾. The exegetes said: (p-447) what you are promised of the Hour, the Resurrection, and the recompense will surely occur, that is, will certainly happen. Then He mentioned when it occurs, saying, exalted is He: ﴿So when the stars are obliterated﴾, that is, their light is effaced; ﴿and when the sky is split open﴾, that is, cleft; ﴿and when the mountains are blown away﴾. al-Zajjaj said: that is, they are all carried off swiftly. It is said: "intasaftu al-shay'" when you seize the thing swiftly.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when the messengers are gathered at their appointed time﴾ (uqqitat). Abu 'Amr recited "wuqqitat" with a waw and a shadda on the qaf. Abu Ja'far agreed with him, except that he lightened the qaf. The rest recited "uqqitat" with an alif in place of the waw and a shadda on the qaf. al-Zajjaj said: "wuqqitat" and "uqqitat" have one meaning. Whoever recited "uqqitat" with a hamza has replaced the hamza for the waw because of the waw's being pointed with a damma. Every waw that takes a damma, and whose damma is inherent, may have a hamza substituted for it. al-Farra' said: when the waw is the first letter and is pointed with a damma, it is made into a hamza; you say: "salla al-qawmu uhdanan." These are fine explanations. The meaning of "uqqitat" is: they were gathered for their time, the Day of Resurrection. Ibn Qutaybah said: they were gathered for a time, which is the Day of Resurrection. al-Zajjaj said: a single time was appointed for them for the separation of judgment among the community.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿For what Day has it been deferred?﴾ That is, it was postponed. The appointing of a term is for their gathering, which amazes the servants at the terror of that Day. Then He explained it, saying, exalted is He: ﴿For the Day of Decision﴾, which is a day on which God, exalted is He, makes the decision among the creatures. Then He magnified that Day by His saying: ﴿And what will make you know what the Day of Decision is?﴾ ﴿Woe on that Day to the deniers﴾ of the Resurrection. Then God, exalted is He, informed of what He did to the denying nations, saying: ﴿Did We not destroy the former peoples?﴾, meaning with punishment in this world when they denied their messengers, ﴿then We follow them with the later ones﴾. The readers recite "nutbi'uhum" with a damma on the ayn, and a group among them, including Abu Haywah, recited with a sukun on the ayn. al-Farra' said: "nutbi'uhum" is in the nominative. This is supported by Ibn Mas'ud's reading "wa-sanutbi'uhumu al-akharin." If you put it in the jussive (jazm), in the sense of "Were We not able to destroy the former ones and follow them with the later ones," it would be a good reading. (p-448) al-Zajjaj said: the jussive is coordinated with "nuhlik," and the meaning would be: for those destroyed first and last. The nominative means: then We follow the first with the last of every criminal. Muqatil said: ﴿then We follow them with the later ones﴾ means the disbelievers of Mecca when they denied the Prophet ﷺ. Ibn Jarir said: the former ones are the people of Noah, 'Ad, and Thamud; the later ones are the people of Abraham, Lot, and Madyan.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Thus do We deal with the criminals﴾, that is, the like of that, meaning the deniers.

If it is asked: what is the benefit of the repetition of His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Woe on that Day to the deniers﴾?

The answer: He intended by each verse of it something other than what He intended by the other, because whenever He mentioned something, He said: "Woe on that Day to the deniers" for this.

This is the Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 77, verses 1–50 (part 2 of 2):

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿This is a day when they will not speak﴾. The exegetes said: This is during some of the stations of the Resurrection. ʿIkrimah said: They spoke and disputed, then a seal was placed upon their mouths, and their hands and their feet spoke, and then they will not speak with any argument that benefits them. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿This is the Day of Decision﴾, that is, between the people of Paradise and the people of Hellfire. ﴿We have gathered you﴾, meaning the deniers of this nation, ﴿and the former peoples﴾ of the deniers who denied their prophets. (p-452) ﴿So if you have a scheme, then scheme against Me﴾. Yaʿqub kept the yaʾ in both states (ALA: fakidūni). That is: if you are able to devise a plan, then devise one for yourselves.

Then He mentioned what belongs to the believers, saying: ﴿Indeed, the God-fearing will be in shades﴾, meaning the shade of trees and the shade of the shelters of palaces, ﴿and springs﴾ of water. This has already been explained, up to His saying: ﴿Eat﴾, that is, it will be said to them: Eat and drink with pleasure for what you used to do in the world by obeying Allah. Then He said to the disbelievers of Makkah: ﴿Eat and enjoy yourselves for a little while﴾ in this world until the end of your appointed terms, ﴿indeed you are criminals﴾, that is, polytheists against Allah.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And when it is said to them, "Bow down"﴾, concerning which there are two views.
The first: that it is when they are called to prostrate on the Day of Resurrection; this was related by al-ʿAwfi from Ibn ʿAbbas.
The second: that in this world, when it was said to them, "Bow down," that is, "Pray," ﴿they do not bow down﴾, that is, they do not pray. Mujahid and others held this view, and it is the most sound. It was also said: it was revealed concerning Thaqif, when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ commanded them to pray, and they said: "We will not bow, for it is a reproach upon us." He said: "There is no good in a religion that has no bowing in it."

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Then in what statement after this will they believe?﴾, that is: if they do not believe in this Qur'an, then in what Book after it will they believe? There is no Book after it.

Completed, by the help and success of Allah the Exalted, is the eighth part of the book "Zad al-Masir fi ʿIlm al-Tafsir" by the Imam Ibn al-Jawzi; and following it is the ninth part, whose beginning is the tafsir of the surah of

(p-443) Surah al-Mursalat (The Emissaries)

It is Meccan in its entirety according to the majority. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah, and Muqatil that it contains one Medinan verse, which is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when it is said to them, "Bow down," they do not bow down﴾ [al-Mursalat: 48].

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿By those sent forth successively﴾ [al-Mursalat: 1]. Regarding it there are four opinions.

The first: they are the winds, following one another. This was narrated by Abu al-'Ubaydayn from Ibn Mas'ud, and by al-'Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas. Mujahid and Qatadah also said this.

The second: they are the angels who are sent with what is good (al-ma'ruf) of God's command and prohibition. This was narrated by Masruq from Ibn Mas'ud. Abu Hurayrah and Muqatil also said this. al-Farra' said: they are the angels.

As for His saying, ﴿successively﴾ ('urfan), it is said: they are sent with what is good, and it is said: they follow one another like the mane (' urf) of a horse. The Arabs say: "The people ride to so-and-so 'urfan wahidan," when they set out towards him in great numbers. Ibn Qutaybah said: he means that the angels follow one another in what they are sent with. Its root is the mane of a horse, because it is a level line, one part following the next, so it was borrowed for a people who follow one another.

(p-445) The third: they are the messengers, by the signs (mu'jizat) by which they are recognized. This is the meaning of the saying of Abu Salih, mentioned by al-Zajjaj.

The fourth: the angels and the wind. This was said by Abu 'Ubaydah, who said: the meaning of "'urfan" is that they follow one another. It is said: "They came to me 'urfan." 

Regarding ﴿the stormy blasts﴾ (al-'asifat) there are two opinions.
One: they are the violently blowing winds. This is what the majority said.
The second: they are the angels. This was said by Muslim ibn Subayh. al-Zajjaj said: they seize (ta'sif) the soul of the disbeliever.

Regarding ﴿those that spread [clouds]﴾ (al-nashirat) there are five opinions.
One: they are the winds that spread the clouds. This was said by Ibn Mas'ud and the majority.
The second: they are the angels that spread the books. This was said by Abu Salih.
The third: the pages (suhuf) that are spread before God, exalted is He, with the deeds of the servants. This was said by al-Dahhak.
The fourth: the resurrection for the Judgment, in which the souls are spread out. This was said by al-Rabi'.
The fifth: the rain, which spreads the vegetation. This is reported by al-Mawardi.

(p-446) Regarding ﴿those that separate [truth from falsehood]﴾ (al-fariqat) there are four opinions.
One: the angels who bring what distinguishes between truth and falsehood. This was said by most of them.
The second: the verses of the Qur'an, which separated between the lawful and the unlawful. This was said by al-Hasan, Qatadah, and Ibn Kaysan.
The third: the wind, which separates the clouds and scatters them. This was said by Mujahid.
The fourth: the messengers. This was reported by al-Zajjaj.

Regarding ﴿those that deliver a reminder﴾ (fa'l-mulqiyat dhikra) there are two opinions.
One: the angels, who deliver to the prophets what they have borne of revelation. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah, and the majority.
The second: the messengers, who convey what was revealed to them to the nations. This was said by Qutrub.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿as an excuse or a warning﴾ ('udhran aw nudhran). Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, and Abu Bakr on the authority of 'Asim recited "'udhran" with a light pronunciation and "nudhran" with a heavy one. Abu 'Amr, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Hafs, and Khalaf recited both "'udhran" and "nudhran" with light pronunciation. al-Farra' said: it is a verbal noun (masdar), whether heavy or light. Its accusative is in the sense: they were sent with what they were sent with as an excuse from God and a warning. al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is: "those that deliver an excuse or a warning." It is also possible that the meaning is: "those that deliver a reminder, as an excuse and a warning." These mentioned things are in the genitive by the oath. The answer to the oath is ﴿What you are promised will surely occur﴾. The exegetes said: (p-447) what you are promised of the Hour, the Resurrection, and the recompense will surely occur, that is, will certainly happen. Then He mentioned when it occurs, saying, exalted is He: ﴿So when the stars are obliterated﴾, that is, their light is effaced; ﴿and when the sky is split open﴾, that is, cleft; ﴿and when the mountains are blown away﴾. al-Zajjaj said: that is, they are all carried off swiftly. It is said: "intasaftu al-shay'" when you seize the thing swiftly.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when the messengers are gathered at their appointed time﴾ (uqqitat). Abu 'Amr recited "wuqqitat" with a waw and a shadda on the qaf. Abu Ja'far agreed with him, except that he lightened the qaf. The rest recited "uqqitat" with an alif in place of the waw and a shadda on the qaf. al-Zajjaj said: "wuqqitat" and "uqqitat" have one meaning. Whoever recited "uqqitat" with a hamza has replaced the hamza for the waw because of the waw's being pointed with a damma. Every waw that takes a damma, and whose damma is inherent, may have a hamza substituted for it. al-Farra' said: when the waw is the first letter and is pointed with a damma, it is made into a hamza; you say: "salla al-qawmu uhdanan." These are fine explanations. The meaning of "uqqitat" is: they were gathered for their time, the Day of Resurrection. Ibn Qutaybah said: they were gathered for a time, which is the Day of Resurrection. al-Zajjaj said: a single time was appointed for them for the separation of judgment among the community.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿For what Day has it been deferred?﴾ That is, it was postponed. The appointing of a term is for their gathering, which amazes the servants at the terror of that Day. Then He explained it, saying, exalted is He: ﴿For the Day of Decision﴾, which is a day on which God, exalted is He, makes the decision among the creatures. Then He magnified that Day by His saying: ﴿And what will make you know what the Day of Decision is?﴾ ﴿Woe on that Day to the deniers﴾ of the Resurrection. Then God, exalted is He, informed of what He did to the denying nations, saying: ﴿Did We not destroy the former peoples?﴾, meaning with punishment in this world when they denied their messengers, ﴿then We follow them with the later ones﴾. The readers recite "nutbi'uhum" with a damma on the ayn, and a group among them, including Abu Haywah, recited with a sukun on the ayn. al-Farra' said: "nutbi'uhum" is in the nominative. This is supported by Ibn Mas'ud's reading "wa-sanutbi'uhumu al-akharin." If you put it in the jussive (jazm), in the sense of "Were We not able to destroy the former ones and follow them with the later ones," it would be a good reading. (p-448) al-Zajjaj said: the jussive is coordinated with "nuhlik," and the meaning would be: for those destroyed first and last. The nominative means: then We follow the first with the last of every criminal. Muqatil said: ﴿then We follow them with the later ones﴾ means the disbelievers of Mecca when they denied the Prophet ﷺ. Ibn Jarir said: the former ones are the people of Noah, 'Ad, and Thamud; the later ones are the people of Abraham, Lot, and Madyan.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Thus do We deal with the criminals﴾, that is, the like of that, meaning the deniers.

If it is asked: what is the benefit of the repetition of His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Woe on that Day to the deniers﴾?

The answer: He intended by each verse of it something other than what He intended by the other, because whenever He mentioned something, He said: "Woe on that Day to the deniers" for this.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Did We not create you﴾. Qalun, on the authority of Nafi', recited with the qaf clearly pronounced (idhhar). The rest recited with its assimilation (idgham).

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿from a despised fluid﴾, that is, weak; ﴿then We placed it in a secure place﴾, meaning the womb; ﴿for a known period﴾, which is the duration of pregnancy; ﴿and We determined [it]﴾. The people of Medina and al-Kisa'i recited "faqaddarna" with a shadda. The rest recited it with a light pronunciation. Is there a difference between them?

Regarding this there are two opinions.
One: they are two dialects with one meaning. al-Farra' said: the Arabs say: "qadara 'alayhi" and "qaddara 'alayhi." Those who recited with the light pronunciation argued: if it were with a shadda, He would have said: "fa-ni'ma al-muqaddirun." al-Farra' answered: the Arabs may combine the two dialects, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So give respite to the disbelievers; give them a little respite﴾ [al-Tariq: 17]. The poet said:

"She denied me, and what she denied was only the graying hair and the baldness."

He says: she denied nothing except what happens among people.

The second: the light form is from "power" (qudrah) and "possession" (milk), and the heavy form is from "measuring" (taqdir) and "decree" (qada'). Then He made clear to them His workmanship so that they might take warning and affirm His oneness. So He said, exalted is He: ﴿Have We not made the earth a gatherer﴾ (kifatan). The linguists said: kaft in the language means gathering together. The meaning is that it gathers its inhabitants, living upon its back and dead in its belly. Ibn Qutaybah said: it is said: "iktif hadha ilayka," that is, gather it to you. They used to call the cemetery of al-Baqi' al-Gharqad "kiftah," because it is a graveyard that gathers the dead.

Regarding His saying, exalted is He: ﴿the living and the dead﴾, there are two opinions.
One: the meaning is: it gathers them, living and dead. This was said by the majority. al-Farra' said: "the living and the dead" are accusative by the falling of the gathering upon them, as if you said: "Have We not made the earth a gathering place of living and dead?" When you put tanwin, you put them in the accusative, as is recited: ﴿or feeding on a day of hunger﴾ ﴿an orphan﴾ [al-Balad: 14]. al-Akhfash said: it is in the accusative as a state (hal).
The second opinion: the meaning is: Have We not made the earth living through vegetation and cultivation, and dead through ruin and dryness? This is the view of Mujahid and Abu 'Ubaydah.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We placed in it firm mountains﴾ (rawasi). The explanation of ﴿towering﴾ (shamikhat), that is, lofty, has already been given. ﴿And We gave you to drink﴾ (asqaynakum): the meaning of "asqayna" has already been given [al-Hijr: 22; al-Jinn: 16], and the meaning of "al-furat" [al-Furqan: 53; Fatir: 12]. The meaning is: these things are more wondrous than resurrection. Then He mentioned what will be said to them in the Hereafter: ﴿Depart to that which you used to deny﴾ in the world, which is the Fire. ﴿Depart to a shade﴾. The majority recited this second word with a kasra on the lam as an imperative. Ubayy ibn Ka'b, (p-450) Abu 'Imran, and Ruways on the authority of Ya'qub recited it with a fatha on the lam as a report in the past tense. Ibn Qutaybah said: "al-zill" here is a shade of the smoke of the Fire of Hell, which rose and then split into three parts; likewise, the nature of great smoke when it rises is that it branches out. It will be said to them: "Remain in it until the reckoning is finished," just as the friends of God are in the shade of His Throne, or wherever He wills of the shade. Then each group is ordered to its place of abode, Paradise or Hell. ﴿Neither shady﴾, that is, it does not shade you from the heat of this Day, but rather brings you near the blaze of the Fire, to what is more severe for you than the heat of the sun. Mujahid said: it will be a branch above the person, a branch on his right, and a branch on his left, encompassing him. al-Dahhak said: the three branches are al-Dari', al-Zaqqum, and al-Ghislin. According to this view, this will be after entering the Fire.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and it will not avail against the flame﴾, that is, it will not ward off from you the blaze of Hell. Then He described the Fire, saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, it throws up sparks﴾, which is the plural of sharrah, that which flies off from the fire, scattered; ﴿like a castle﴾ (al-qasr). The majority recited with a sukun on the sad, as the singular of the palaces (qusur) that are built. This meaning is in the narration of Ibn Abi Talhah from Ibn 'Abbas, and it is the view of the majority. Ibn 'Abbas, Abu Razin, Mujahid, and Abu al-Jawza' recited "kal-qasar" with a fatha on the sad. In the singular reports of al-Bukhari from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas, he said: "We used to lift wood, a cask of three cubits or less, and lift it for winter, and we called it al-qasar." Ibn Qutaybah said: by the fatha on the sad he meant the roots of cut palm trees, uprooted. al-Zajjaj said: he meant the necks of camels. Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, 'A'ishah, 'Ikrimah, Abu Mijlaz, Abu al-Mutawakkil, and Ibn Ya'mar recited "kal-qasir" with a fatha on the qaf and a kasra on the sad. Ibn Mas'ud, Abu Hurayrah, and al-Nakha'i recited "kal-qusur" with a damma on both the qaf and the sad. Abu al-Darda', and Sa'id ibn (p-451) Jubayr recited "kal-qisar" with a kasra on the qaf and a fatha on the sad. Abu al-'Aliyah, Abu 'Imran, Abu Nuhayk, and Mu'adh al-Qari' recited "kal-qusr" with a damma on the qaf and a sukun on the sad.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿As if they were yellow camels﴾ (jimalatun). Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, and Abu Bakr on the authority of 'Asim recited "jimalatun" with an alif and a kasra on the jim. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Hafs on the authority of 'Asim recited "jimalatun" in the singular. Ruways on the authority of Ya'qub recited "jumalatun" with a damma on the jim. Abu Razin, Humayd, and Abu Haywah recited "jumalatun" with a damma on the jim in the singular. al-Zajjaj said: whoever recited "jimalatun" with a kasra is the plural of jimal, as you say: buyut and buyutat, and it is the plural of the plural, so the meaning is: as if the sparks were like the camels. Whoever recited "jumalatun" with a damma is the plural of "jumalah," and whoever recited "jumalatun" is the plural of jamal and jimalah, as it is said: hajar and hijarah, and dhakar and dhikarah. And "jumalatun" has been read, in the manner we explained, as "jumalatun" with a damma. And "al-sufr" here means the black ones. It is said of black camels that tend toward yellow: "ibil sufr." al-Farra' said: "al-sufr" are the black camels; a black camel is never seen except that it has a tinge of yellow, and so the Arabs called black camels "sufr," just as they called gazelles "adam" because of the darkness that overspreads their whiteness.

This is the Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 77, verses 1–50 (part 2 of 2):

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿This is a day when they will not speak﴾. The exegetes said: This is during some of the stations of the Resurrection. ʿIkrimah said: They spoke and disputed, then a seal was placed upon their mouths, and their hands and their feet spoke, and then they will not speak with any argument that benefits them. Abu Rajaʾ, al-Qasim ibn Muhammad, al-Aʿmash, and Ibn Abi ʿAblah read "This is a day when they will not speak" with a fatha on the mim (ALA: yawma, in the accusative).

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿This is the Day of Decision﴾, that is, between the people of Paradise and the people of Hellfire. ﴿We have gathered you﴾, meaning the deniers of this nation, ﴿and the former peoples﴾ of the deniers who denied their prophets. (p-452) ﴿So if you have a scheme, then scheme against Me﴾. Yaʿqub kept the yaʾ in both states (ALA: fakidūni). That is: if you are able to devise a plan, then devise one for yourselves.

Then He mentioned what belongs to the believers, saying: ﴿Indeed, the God-fearing will be in shades﴾, meaning the shade of trees and the shade of the shelters of palaces, ﴿and springs﴾ of water. This has already been explained, up to His saying: ﴿Eat﴾, that is, it will be said to them: Eat and drink with pleasure for what you used to do in the world by obeying Allah. Then He said to the disbelievers of Makkah: ﴿Eat and enjoy yourselves for a little while﴾ in this world until the end of your appointed terms, ﴿indeed you are criminals﴾, that is, polytheists against Allah.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And when it is said to them, "Bow down"﴾, concerning which there are two views.
The first: that it is when they are called to prostrate on the Day of Resurrection; this was related by al-ʿAwfi from Ibn ʿAbbas.
The second: that in this world, when it was said to them, "Bow down," that is, "Pray," ﴿they do not bow down﴾, that is, they do not pray. Mujahid and others held this view, and it is the most sound. It was also said: it was revealed concerning Thaqif, when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ commanded them to pray, and they said: "We will not bow, for it is a reproach upon us." He said: "There is no good in a religion that has no bowing in it."

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Then in what statement after this will they believe?﴾, that is: if they do not believe in this Qur'an, then in what Book after it will they believe? There is no Book after it.

Then He magnified that Day by His saying: ﴿And what will make you know what the Day of Decision is?﴾ ﴿Woe on that Day to the deniers﴾ of the Resurrection. The readers recite "nutbi'uhum" with a damma on the ayn, and a group among them, including Abu Haywah, recited with a sukun on the ayn. al-Farra' said: "nutbi'uhum" is in the nominative. This is supported by Ibn Mas'ud's reading "wa-sanutbi'uhumu al-akharin." If you put it in the jussive (jazm), in the sense of "Were We not able to destroy the former ones and follow them with the later ones," it would be a good reading. (p-448) al-Zajjaj said: the jussive is coordinated with "nuhlik," and the meaning would be: for those destroyed first and last. The nominative means: then We follow the first with the last of every criminal. Muqatil said: ﴿then We follow them with the later ones﴾ means the disbelievers of Mecca when they denied the Prophet ﷺ. Ibn Jarir said: the former ones are the people of Noah, 'Ad, and Thamud; the later ones are the people of Abraham, Lot, and Madyan.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Thus do We deal with the criminals﴾, that is, the like of that, meaning the deniers.

If it is asked: what is the benefit of the repetition of His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Woe on that Day to the deniers﴾?

The answer: He intended by each verse of it something other than what He intended by the other, because whenever He mentioned something, He said: "Woe on that Day to the deniers" for this.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Did We not create you﴾. Qalun, on the authority of Nafi', recited with the qaf clearly pronounced (idhhar). The rest recited with its assimilation (idgham).

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿from a despised fluid﴾, that is, weak; ﴿then We placed it in a secure place﴾, meaning the womb; ﴿for a known period﴾, which is the duration of pregnancy; ﴿and We determined [it]﴾. The people of Medina and al-Kisa'i recited "faqaddarna" with a shadda. The rest recited it with a light pronunciation. Is there a difference between them?

Regarding this there are two opinions.
One: they are two dialects with one meaning. al-Farra' said: the Arabs say: "qadara 'alayhi" and "qaddara 'alayhi." Those who recited with the light pronunciation argued: if it were with a shadda, He would have said: "fa-ni'ma al-muqaddirun." al-Farra' answered: the Arabs may combine the two dialects, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So give respite to the disbelievers; give them a little respite﴾ [al-Tariq: 17]. The poet said:

"She denied me, and what she denied was only the graying hair and the baldness."

He says: she denied nothing except what happens among people.

The second: the light form is from "power" (qudrah) and "possession" (milk), and the heavy form is from "measuring" (taqdir) and "decree" (qada'). Then He made clear to them His workmanship so that they might take warning and affirm His oneness. So He said, exalted is He: ﴿Have We not made the earth a gatherer﴾ (kifatan). The linguists said: kaft in the language means gathering together. The meaning is that it gathers its inhabitants, living upon its back and dead in its belly. Ibn Qutaybah said: it is said: "iktif hadha ilayka," that is, gather it to you. They used to call the cemetery of al-Baqi' al-Gharqad "kiftah," because it is a graveyard that gathers the dead.

Regarding His saying, exalted is He: ﴿the living and the dead﴾, there are two opinions.
One: the meaning is: it gathers them, living and dead. This was said by the majority. al-Farra' said: "the living and the dead" are accusative by the falling of the gathering upon them, as if you said: "Have We not made the earth a gathering place of living and dead?" When you put tanwin, you put them in the accusative, as is recited: ﴿or feeding on a day of hunger﴾ ﴿an orphan﴾ [al-Balad: 14]. al-Akhfash said: it is in the accusative as a state (hal).
The second opinion: the meaning is: Have We not made the earth living through vegetation and cultivation, and dead through ruin and dryness? This is the view of Mujahid and Abu 'Ubaydah.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We placed in it firm mountains﴾ (rawasi). The explanation of ﴿towering﴾ (shamikhat), that is, lofty, has already been given. ﴿And We gave you to drink﴾ (asqaynakum): the meaning of "asqayna" has already been given [al-Hijr: 22; al-Jinn: 16], and the meaning of "al-furat" [al-Furqan: 53; Fatir: 12]. The meaning is: these things are more wondrous than resurrection. Then He mentioned what will be said to them in the Hereafter: ﴿Depart to that which you used to deny﴾ in the world, which is the Fire. ﴿Depart to a shade﴾. The majority recited this second word with a kasra on the lam as an imperative. Ubayy ibn Ka'b, (p-450) Abu 'Imran, and Ruways on the authority of Ya'qub recited it with a fatha on the lam as a report in the past tense. Ibn Qutaybah said: "al-zill" here is a shade of the smoke of the Fire of Hell, which rose and then split into three parts; likewise, the nature of great smoke when it rises is that it branches out. It will be said to them: "Remain in it until the reckoning is finished," just as the friends of God are in the shade of His Throne, or wherever He wills of the shade. Then each group is ordered to its place of abode, Paradise or Hell. ﴿Neither shady﴾, that is, it does not shade you from the heat of this Day, but rather brings you near the blaze of the Fire, to what is more severe for you than the heat of the sun. Mujahid said: it will be a branch above the person, a branch on his right, and a branch on his left, encompassing him. al-Dahhak said: the three branches are al-Dari', al-Zaqqum, and al-Ghislin. According to this view, this will be after entering the Fire.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and it will not avail against the flame﴾, that is, it will not ward off from you the blaze of Hell. Then He described the Fire, saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, it throws up sparks﴾, which is the plural of sharrah, that which flies off from the fire, scattered; ﴿like a castle﴾ (al-qasr). The majority recited with a sukun on the sad, as the singular of the palaces (qusur) that are built. This meaning is in the narration of Ibn Abi Talhah from Ibn 'Abbas, and it is the view of the majority. Ibn 'Abbas, Abu Razin, Mujahid, and Abu al-Jawza' recited "kal-qasar" with a fatha on the sad. In the singular reports of al-Bukhari from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas, he said: "We used to lift wood, a cask of three cubits or less, and lift it for winter, and we called it al-qasar." Ibn Qutaybah said: by the fatha on the sad he meant the roots of cut palm trees, uprooted. al-Zajjaj said: he meant the necks of camels. Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, 'A'ishah, 'Ikrimah, Abu Mijlaz, Abu al-Mutawakkil, and Ibn Ya'mar recited "kal-qasir" with a fatha on the qaf and a kasra on the sad. Ibn Mas'ud, Abu Hurayrah, and al-Nakha'i recited "kal-qusur" with a damma on both the qaf and the sad. Abu al-Darda', and Sa'id ibn (p-451) Jubayr recited "kal-qisar" with a kasra on the qaf and a fatha on the sad. Abu al-'Aliyah, Abu 'Imran, Abu Nuhayk, and Mu'adh al-Qari' recited "kal-qusr" with a damma on the qaf and a sukun on the sad.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿As if they were yellow camels﴾ (jimalatun). Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, and Abu Bakr on the authority of 'Asim recited "jimalatun" with an alif and a kasra on the jim. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Hafs on the authority of 'Asim recited "jimalatun" in the singular. Ruways on the authority of Ya'qub recited "jumalatun" with a damma on the jim. Abu Razin, Humayd, and Abu Haywah recited "jumalatun" with a damma on the jim in the singular. al-Zajjaj said: whoever recited "jimalatun" with a kasra is the plural of jimal, as you say: buyut and buyutat, and it is the plural of the plural, so the meaning is: as if the sparks were like the camels. Whoever recited "jumalatun" with a damma is the plural of "jumalah," and whoever recited "jumalatun" is the plural of jamal and jimalah, as it is said: hajar and hijarah, and dhakar and dhikarah. And "jumalatun" has been read, in the manner we explained, as "jumalatun" with a damma. And "al-sufr" here means the black ones. It is said of black camels that tend toward yellow: "ibil sufr." al-Farra' said: "al-sufr" are the black camels; a black camel is never seen except that it has a tinge of yellow, and so the Arabs called black camels "sufr," just as they called gazelles "adam" because of the darkness that overspreads their whiteness.

This is the Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 77, verses 1–50 (part 2 of 2):

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿This is a day when they will not speak﴾. The exegetes said: This is during some of the stations of the Resurrection. ʿIkrimah said: They spoke and disputed, then a seal was placed upon their mouths, and their hands and their feet spoke, and then they will not speak with any argument that benefits them. Abu Rajaʾ, al-Qasim ibn Muhammad, al-Aʿmash, and Ibn Abi ʿAblah read "This is a day when they will not speak" with a fatha on the mim (ALA: yawma, in the accusative).

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿This is the Day of Decision﴾, that is, between the people of Paradise and the people of Hellfire. ﴿We have gathered you﴾, meaning the deniers of this nation, ﴿and the former peoples﴾ of the deniers who denied their prophets. (p-452) ﴿So if you have a scheme, then scheme against Me﴾. Yaʿqub kept the yaʾ in both states (ALA: fakidūni). That is: if you are able to devise a plan, then devise one for yourselves.

Then He mentioned what belongs to the believers, saying: ﴿Indeed, the God-fearing will be in shades﴾, meaning the shade of trees and the shade of the shelters of palaces, ﴿and springs﴾ of water. This has already been explained, up to His saying: ﴿Eat﴾, that is, it will be said to them: Eat and drink with pleasure for what you used to do in the world by obeying Allah. Then He said to the disbelievers of Makkah: ﴿Eat and enjoy yourselves for a little while﴾ in this world until the end of your appointed terms, ﴿indeed you are criminals﴾, that is, polytheists against Allah.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And when it is said to them, "Bow down"﴾, concerning which there are two views.
The first: that it is when they are called to prostrate on the Day of Resurrection; this was related by al-ʿAwfi from Ibn ʿAbbas.
The second: that in this world, when it was said to them, "Bow down," that is, "Pray," ﴿they do not bow down﴾, that is, they do not pray. Mujahid and others held this view, and it is the most sound. It was also said: it was revealed concerning Thaqif, when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ commanded them to pray, and they said: "We will not bow, for it is a reproach upon us." He said: "There is no good in a religion that has no bowing in it."

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Then in what statement after this will they believe?﴾, that is: if they do not believe in this Qur'an, then in what Book after it will they believe? There is no Book after it.

Completed, by the help and success of Allah the Exalted, is the eighth part of the book "Zad al-Masir fi ʿIlm al-Tafsir" by the Imam Ibn al-Jawzi; and following it is the ninth part, whose beginning is the tafsir of the surah of

(p-443) Surah al-Mursalat (The Emissaries)

It is Meccan in its entirety according to the majority. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah, and Muqatil that it contains one Medinan verse, which is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when it is said to them, "Bow down," they do not bow down﴾ [al-Mursalat: 48].

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿By those sent forth successively﴾ [al-Mursalat: 1]. Regarding it there are four opinions.

The first: they are the winds, following one another. This was narrated by Abu al-'Ubaydayn from Ibn Mas'ud, and by al-'Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas. Mujahid and Qatadah also said this.

The second: they are the angels who are sent with what is good (al-ma'ruf) of God's command and prohibition. This was narrated by Masruq from Ibn Mas'ud. Abu Hurayrah and Muqatil also said this. al-Farra' said: they are the angels.

As for His saying, ﴿successively﴾ ('urfan), it is said: they are sent with what is good, and it is said: they follow one another like the mane (' urf) of a horse. The Arabs say: "The people ride to so-and-so 'urfan wahidan," when they set out towards him in great numbers. Ibn Qutaybah said: he means that the angels follow one another in what they are sent with. Its root is the mane of a horse, because it is a level line, one part following the next, so it was borrowed for a people who follow one another.

(p-445) The third: they are the messengers, by the signs (mu'jizat) by which they are recognized. This is the meaning of the saying of Abu Salih, mentioned by al-Zajjaj.

The fourth: the angels and the wind. This was said by Abu 'Ubaydah, who said: the meaning of "'urfan" is that they follow one another. It is said: "They came to me 'urfan." 

Regarding ﴿the stormy blasts﴾ (al-'asifat) there are two opinions.
One: they are the violently blowing winds. This is what the majority said.
The second: they are the angels. This was said by Muslim ibn Subayh. al-Zajjaj said: they seize (ta'sif) the soul of the disbeliever.

Regarding ﴿those that spread [clouds]﴾ (al-nashirat) there are five opinions.
One: they are the winds that spread the clouds. This was said by Ibn Mas'ud and the majority.
The second: they are the angels that spread the books. This was said by Abu Salih.
The third: the pages (suhuf) that are spread before God, exalted is He, with the deeds of the servants. This was said by al-Dahhak.
The fourth: the resurrection for the Judgment, in which the souls are spread out. This was said by al-Rabi'.
The fifth: the rain, which spreads the vegetation. This is reported by al-Mawardi.

(p-446) Regarding ﴿those that separate [truth from falsehood]﴾ (al-fariqat) there are four opinions.
One: the angels who bring what distinguishes between truth and falsehood. This was said by most of them.
The second: the verses of the Qur'an, which separated between the lawful and the unlawful. This was said by al-Hasan, Qatadah, and Ibn Kaysan.
The third: the wind, which separates the clouds and scatters them. This was said by Mujahid.
The fourth: the messengers. This was reported by al-Zajjaj.

Regarding ﴿those that deliver a reminder﴾ (fa'l-mulqiyat dhikra) there are two opinions.
One: the angels, who deliver to the prophets what they have borne of revelation. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah, and the majority.
The second: the messengers, who convey what was revealed to them to the nations. This was said by Qutrub.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿as an excuse or a warning﴾ ('udhran aw nudhran). Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, and Abu Bakr on the authority of 'Asim recited "'udhran" with a light pronunciation and "nudhran" with a heavy one. Abu 'Amr, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Hafs, and Khalaf recited both "'udhran" and "nudhran" with light pronunciation. al-Farra' said: it is a verbal noun (masdar), whether heavy or light. Its accusative is in the sense: they were sent with what they were sent with as an excuse from God and a warning. al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is: "those that deliver an excuse or a warning." It is also possible that the meaning is: "those that deliver a reminder, as an excuse and a warning." These mentioned things are in the genitive by the oath. The answer to the oath is ﴿What you are promised will surely occur﴾. The exegetes said: (p-447) what you are promised of the Hour, the Resurrection, and the recompense will surely occur, that is, will certainly happen. Then He mentioned when it occurs, saying, exalted is He: ﴿So when the stars are obliterated﴾, that is, their light is effaced; ﴿and when the sky is split open﴾, that is, cleft; ﴿and when the mountains are blown away﴾. al-Zajjaj said: that is, they are all carried off swiftly. It is said: "intasaftu al-shay'" when you seize the thing swiftly.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when the messengers are gathered at their appointed time﴾ (uqqitat). Abu 'Amr recited "wuqqitat" with a waw and a shadda on the qaf. Abu Ja'far agreed with him, except that he lightened the qaf. The rest recited "uqqitat" with an alif in place of the waw and a shadda on the qaf. al-Zajjaj said: "wuqqitat" and "uqqitat" have one meaning. Whoever recited "uqqitat" with a hamza has replaced the hamza for the waw because of the waw's being pointed with a damma. Every waw that takes a damma, and whose damma is inherent, may have a hamza substituted for it. al-Farra' said: when the waw is the first letter and is pointed with a damma, it is made into a hamza; you say: "salla al-qawmu uhdanan." These are fine explanations. The meaning of "uqqitat" is: they were gathered for their time, the Day of Resurrection. Ibn Qutaybah said: they were gathered for a time, which is the Day of Resurrection. al-Zajjaj said: a single time was appointed for them for the separation of judgment among the community.

Then He explained it, saying, exalted is He: ﴿For the Day of Decision﴾, which is a day on which God, exalted is He, makes the decision among the creatures. Then He magnified that Day by His saying: ﴿And what will make you know what the Day of Decision is?﴾ ﴿Woe on that Day to the deniers﴾ of the Resurrection. Abu Razin, Humayd, and Abu Haywah recited "jumalatun" with a damma on the jim in the singular. al-Zajjaj said: whoever recited "jimalatun" with a kasra is the plural of jimal, as you say: buyut and buyutat, and it is the plural of the plural, so the meaning is: as if the sparks were like the camels. And "jumalatun" has been read, in the manner we explained, as "jumalatun" with a damma. And "al-sufr" here means the black ones. It is said of black camels that tend toward yellow: "ibil sufr." al-Farra' said: "al-sufr" are the black camels; a black camel is never seen except that it has a tinge of yellow, and so the Arabs called black camels "sufr," just as they called gazelles "adam" because of the darkness that overspreads their whiteness.

This is the Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 77, verses 1–50 (part 2 of 2):

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿This is a day when they will not speak﴾. The exegetes said: This is during some of the stations of the Resurrection. ʿIkrimah said: They spoke and disputed, then a seal was placed upon their mouths, and their hands and their feet spoke, and then they will not speak with any argument that benefits them. Abu Rajaʾ, al-Qasim ibn Muhammad, al-Aʿmash, and Ibn Abi ʿAblah read "This is a day when they will not speak" with a fatha on the mim (ALA: yawma, in the accusative).

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿This is the Day of Decision﴾, that is, between the people of Paradise and the people of Hellfire. ﴿We have gathered you﴾, meaning the deniers of this nation, ﴿and the former peoples﴾ of the deniers who denied their prophets. (p-452) ﴿So if you have a scheme, then scheme against Me﴾. Yaʿqub kept the yaʾ in both states (ALA: fakidūni). That is: if you are able to devise a plan, then devise one for yourselves.

Then He mentioned what belongs to the believers, saying: ﴿Indeed, the God-fearing will be in shades﴾, meaning the shade of trees and the shade of the shelters of palaces, ﴿and springs﴾ of water. This has already been explained, up to His saying: ﴿Eat﴾, that is, it will be said to them: Eat and drink with pleasure for what you used to do in the world by obeying Allah. Then He said to the disbelievers of Makkah: ﴿Eat and enjoy yourselves for a little while﴾ in this world until the end of your appointed terms, ﴿indeed you are criminals﴾, that is, polytheists against Allah.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And when it is said to them, "Bow down"﴾, concerning which there are two views.
The first: that it is when they are called to prostrate on the Day of Resurrection; this was related by al-ʿAwfi from Ibn ʿAbbas.
The second: that in this world, when it was said to them, "Bow down," that is, "Pray," ﴿they do not bow down﴾, that is, they do not pray. Mujahid and others held this view, and it is the most sound. It was also said: it was revealed concerning Thaqif, when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ commanded them to pray, and they said: "We will not bow, for it is a reproach upon us." He said: "There is no good in a religion that has no bowing in it."

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Then in what statement after this will they believe?﴾, that is: if they do not believe in this Qur'an, then in what Book after it will they believe? There is no Book after it.

Completed, by the help and success of Allah the Exalted, is the eighth part of the book "Zad al-Masir fi ʿIlm al-Tafsir" by the Imam Ibn al-Jawzi; and following it is the ninth part, whose beginning is the tafsir of the surah of

(p-443) Surah al-Mursalat (The Emissaries)

It is Meccan in its entirety according to the majority. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah, and Muqatil that it contains one Medinan verse, which is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when it is said to them, "Bow down," they do not bow down﴾ [al-Mursalat: 48].

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿By those sent forth successively﴾ [al-Mursalat: 1]. Regarding it there are four opinions.

The first: they are the winds, following one another. This was narrated by Abu al-'Ubaydayn from Ibn Mas'ud, and by al-'Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas. Mujahid and Qatadah also said this.

The second: they are the angels who are sent with what is good (al-ma'ruf) of God's command and prohibition. This was narrated by Masruq from Ibn Mas'ud. Abu Hurayrah and Muqatil also said this. al-Farra' said: they are the angels.

As for His saying, ﴿successively﴾ ('urfan), it is said: they are sent with what is good, and it is said: they follow one another like the mane (' urf) of a horse. The Arabs say: "The people ride to so-and-so 'urfan wahidan," when they set out towards him in great numbers. Ibn Qutaybah said: he means that the angels follow one another in what they are sent with. Its root is the mane of a horse, because it is a level line, one part following the next, so it was borrowed for a people who follow one another.

(p-445) The third: they are the messengers, by the signs (mu'jizat) by which they are recognized. This is the meaning of the saying of Abu Salih, mentioned by al-Zajjaj.

The fourth: the angels and the wind. This was said by Abu 'Ubaydah, who said: the meaning of "'urfan" is that they follow one another. It is said: "They came to me 'urfan." 

Regarding ﴿the stormy blasts﴾ (al-'asifat) there are two opinions.
One: they are the violently blowing winds. This is what the majority said.
The second: they are the angels. This was said by Muslim ibn Subayh. al-Zajjaj said: they seize (ta'sif) the soul of the disbeliever.

Regarding ﴿those that spread [clouds]﴾ (al-nashirat) there are five opinions.
One: they are the winds that spread the clouds. This was said by Ibn Mas'ud and the majority.
The second: they are the angels that spread the books. This was said by Abu Salih.
The third: the pages (suhuf) that are spread before God, exalted is He, with the deeds of the servants. This was said by al-Dahhak.
The fourth: the resurrection for the Judgment, in which the souls are spread out. This was said by al-Rabi'.
The fifth: the rain, which spreads the vegetation. This is reported by al-Mawardi.

(p-446) Regarding ﴿those that separate [truth from falsehood]﴾ (al-fariqat) there are four opinions.
One: the angels who bring what distinguishes between truth and falsehood. This was said by most of them.
The second: the verses of the Qur'an, which separated between the lawful and the unlawful. This was said by al-Hasan, Qatadah, and Ibn Kaysan.
The third: the wind, which separates the clouds and scatters them. This was said by Mujahid.
The fourth: the messengers. This was reported by al-Zajjaj.

Regarding ﴿those that deliver a reminder﴾ (fa'l-mulqiyat dhikra) there are two opinions.
One: the angels, who deliver to the prophets what they have borne of revelation. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah, and the majority.
The second: the messengers, who convey what was revealed to them to the nations. This was said by Qutrub.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿as an excuse or a warning﴾ ('udhran aw nudhran). Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, and Abu Bakr on the authority of 'Asim recited "'udhran" with a light pronunciation and "nudhran" with a heavy one. Abu 'Amr, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Hafs, and Khalaf recited both "'udhran" and "nudhran" with light pronunciation. al-Farra' said: it is a verbal noun (masdar), whether heavy or light. Its accusative is in the sense: they were sent with what they were sent with as an excuse from God and a warning. al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is: "those that deliver an excuse or a warning." It is also possible that the meaning is: "those that deliver a reminder, as an excuse and a warning." These mentioned things are in the genitive by the oath. The answer to the oath is ﴿What you are promised will surely occur﴾. The exegetes said: (p-447) what you are promised of the Hour, the Resurrection, and the recompense will surely occur, that is, will certainly happen. Then He mentioned when it occurs, saying, exalted is He: ﴿So when the stars are obliterated﴾, that is, their light is effaced; ﴿and when the sky is split open﴾, that is, cleft; ﴿and when the mountains are blown away﴾. al-Zajjaj said: that is, they are all carried off swiftly. It is said: "intasaftu al-shay'" when you seize the thing swiftly.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when the messengers are gathered at their appointed time﴾ (uqqitat). Abu 'Amr recited "wuqqitat" with a waw and a shadda on the qaf. Abu Ja'far agreed with him, except that he lightened the qaf. The rest recited "uqqitat" with an alif in place of the waw and a shadda on the qaf. al-Zajjaj said: "wuqqitat" and "uqqitat" have one meaning. Whoever recited "uqqitat" with a hamza has replaced the hamza for the waw because of the waw's being pointed with a damma. Every waw that takes a damma, and whose damma is inherent, may have a hamza substituted for it. al-Farra' said: when the waw is the first letter and is pointed with a damma, it is made into a hamza; you say: "salla al-qawmu uhdanan." These are fine explanations. The meaning of "uqqitat" is: they were gathered for their time, the Day of Resurrection. Ibn Qutaybah said: they were gathered for a time, which is the Day of Resurrection. al-Zajjaj said: a single time was appointed for them for the separation of judgment among the community.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿For what Day has it been deferred?﴾ That is, it was postponed. The appointing of a term is for their gathering, which amazes the servants at the terror of that Day. Then He explained it, saying, exalted is He: ﴿For the Day of Decision﴾, which is a day on which God, exalted is He, makes the decision among the creatures. Then He magnified that Day by His saying: ﴿And what will make you know what the Day of Decision is?﴾ ﴿Woe on that Day to the deniers﴾ of the Resurrection. Then God, exalted is He, informed of what He did to the denying nations, saying: ﴿Did We not destroy the former peoples?﴾, meaning with punishment in this world when they denied their messengers, ﴿then We follow them with the later ones﴾. The readers recite "nutbi'uhum" with a damma on the ayn, and a group among them, including Abu Haywah, recited with a sukun on the ayn. al-Farra' said: "nutbi'uhum" is in the nominative. This is supported by Ibn Mas'ud's reading "wa-sanutbi'uhumu al-akharin." If you put it in the jussive (jazm), in the sense of "Were We not able to destroy the former ones and follow them with the later ones," it would be a good reading. (p-448) al-Zajjaj said: the jussive is coordinated with "nuhlik," and the meaning would be: for those destroyed first and last. The nominative means: then We follow the first with the last of every criminal. Muqatil said: ﴿then We follow them with the later ones﴾ means the disbelievers of Mecca when they denied the Prophet ﷺ. Ibn Jarir said: the former ones are the people of Noah, 'Ad, and Thamud; the later ones are the people of Abraham, Lot, and Madyan.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Thus do We deal with the criminals﴾, that is, the like of that, meaning the deniers.

If it is asked: what is the benefit of the repetition of His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Woe on that Day to the deniers﴾?

The answer: He intended by each verse of it something other than what He intended by the other, because whenever He mentioned something, He said: "Woe on that Day to the deniers" for this.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Did We not create you﴾. Qalun, on the authority of Nafi', recited with the qaf clearly pronounced (idhhar). The rest recited with its assimilation (idgham).

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿from a despised fluid﴾, that is, weak; ﴿then We placed it in a secure place﴾, meaning the womb; ﴿for a known period﴾, which is the duration of pregnancy; ﴿and We determined [it]﴾. The people of Medina and al-Kisa'i recited "faqaddarna" with a shadda. The rest recited it with a light pronunciation. Is there a difference between them?

Regarding this there are two opinions.
One: they are two dialects with one meaning. al-Farra' said: the Arabs say: "qadara 'alayhi" and "qaddara 'alayhi." Those who recited with the light pronunciation argued: if it were with a shadda, He would have said: "fa-ni'ma al-muqaddirun." al-Farra' answered: the Arabs may combine the two dialects, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So give respite to the disbelievers; give them a little respite﴾ [al-Tariq: 17]. The poet said:

"She denied me, and what she denied was only the graying hair and the baldness."

He says: she denied nothing except what happens among people.

The second: the light form is from "power" (qudrah) and "possession" (milk), and the heavy form is from "measuring" (taqdir) and "decree" (qada'). Then He made clear to them His workmanship so that they might take warning and affirm His oneness. So He said, exalted is He: ﴿Have We not made the earth a gatherer﴾ (kifatan). The linguists said: kaft in the language means gathering together. The meaning is that it gathers its inhabitants, living upon its back and dead in its belly. Ibn Qutaybah said: it is said: "iktif hadha ilayka," that is, gather it to you. They used to call the cemetery of al-Baqi' al-Gharqad "kiftah," because it is a graveyard that gathers the dead.

Regarding His saying, exalted is He: ﴿the living and the dead﴾, there are two opinions.
One: the meaning is: it gathers them, living and dead. This was said by the majority. al-Farra' said: "the living and the dead" are accusative by the falling of the gathering upon them, as if you said: "Have We not made the earth a gathering place of living and dead?" When you put tanwin, you put them in the accusative, as is recited: ﴿or feeding on a day of hunger﴾ ﴿an orphan﴾ [al-Balad: 14]. al-Akhfash said: it is in the accusative as a state (hal).
The second opinion: the meaning is: Have We not made the earth living through vegetation and cultivation, and dead through ruin and dryness? This is the view of Mujahid and Abu 'Ubaydah.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We placed in it firm mountains﴾ (rawasi). The explanation of ﴿towering﴾ (shamikhat), that is, lofty, has already been given. ﴿And We gave you to drink﴾ (asqaynakum): the meaning of "asqayna" has already been given [al-Hijr: 22; al-Jinn: 16], and the meaning of "al-furat" [al-Furqan: 53; Fatir: 12]. The meaning is: these things are more wondrous than resurrection. Then He mentioned what will be said to them in the Hereafter: ﴿Depart to that which you used to deny﴾ in the world, which is the Fire. ﴿Depart to a shade﴾. The majority recited this second word with a kasra on the lam as an imperative. Ubayy ibn Ka'b, (p-450) Abu 'Imran, and Ruways on the authority of Ya'qub recited it with a fatha on the lam as a report in the past tense. Ibn Qutaybah said: "al-zill" here is a shade of the smoke of the Fire of Hell, which rose and then split into three parts; likewise, the nature of great smoke when it rises is that it branches out. It will be said to them: "Remain in it until the reckoning is finished," just as the friends of God are in the shade of His Throne, or wherever He wills of the shade. Then each group is ordered to its place of abode, Paradise or Hell. ﴿Neither shady﴾, that is, it does not shade you from the heat of this Day, but rather brings you near the blaze of the Fire, to what is more severe for you than the heat of the sun. Mujahid said: it will be a branch above the person, a branch on his right, and a branch on his left, encompassing him. al-Dahhak said: the three branches are al-Dari', al-Zaqqum, and al-Ghislin. According to this view, this will be after entering the Fire.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and it will not avail against the flame﴾, that is, it will not ward off from you the blaze of Hell. Then He described the Fire, saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, it throws up sparks﴾, which is the plural of sharrah, that which flies off from the fire, scattered; ﴿like a castle﴾ (al-qasr). The majority recited with a sukun on the sad, as the singular of the palaces (qusur) that are built. This meaning is in the narration of Ibn Abi Talhah from Ibn 'Abbas, and it is the view of the majority. Ibn 'Abbas, Abu Razin, Mujahid, and Abu al-Jawza' recited "kal-qasar" with a fatha on the sad. In the singular reports of al-Bukhari from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas, he said: "We used to lift wood, a cask of three cubits or less, and lift it for winter, and we called it al-qasar." Ibn Qutaybah said: by the fatha on the sad he meant the roots of cut palm trees, uprooted. al-Zajjaj said: he meant the necks of camels. Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, 'A'ishah, 'Ikrimah, Abu Mijlaz, Abu al-Mutawakkil, and Ibn Ya'mar recited "kal-qasir" with a fatha on the qaf and a kasra on the sad. Ibn Mas'ud, Abu Hurayrah, and al-Nakha'i recited "kal-qusur" with a damma on both the qaf and the sad. Abu al-Darda', and Sa'id ibn (p-451) Jubayr recited "kal-qisar" with a kasra on the qaf and a fatha on the sad. Abu al-'Aliyah, Abu 'Imran, Abu Nuhayk, and Mu'adh al-Qari' recited "kal-qusr" with a damma on the qaf and a sukun on the sad.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿As if they were yellow camels﴾ (jimalatun). Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, and Abu Bakr on the authority of 'Asim recited "jimalatun" with an alif and a kasra on the jim. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Hafs on the authority of 'Asim recited "jimalatun" in the singular. Ruways on the authority of Ya'qub recited "jumalatun" with a damma on the jim. Abu Razin, Humayd, and Abu Haywah recited "jumalatun" with a damma on the jim in the singular. al-Zajjaj said: whoever recited "jimalatun" with a kasra is the plural of jimal, as you say: buyut and buyutat, and it is the plural of the plural, so the meaning is: as if the sparks were like the camels. Whoever recited "jumalatun" with a damma is the plural of "jumalah," and whoever recited "jumalatun" is the plural of jamal and jimalah, as it is said: hajar and hijarah, and dhakar and dhikarah. And "jumalatun" has been read, in the manner we explained, as "jumalatun" with a damma. And "al-sufr" here means the black ones.
